title: What low-level design is
idea: Low-level design is deciding the classes, their responsibilities, their methods and how they talk to each other, before or while you write the code.
points: High-level design picks services and databases; low-level design shapes the code inside one service.
You start from requirements and find the nouns: they become candidate classes.
Each class gets one clear job and a small public surface of methods.
Interviews judge whether your classes are easy to extend, test and explain.

edges.label: find nouns
edges.caption: Read the requirements and list the nouns. A garage, its slots and the tickets it issues.

edges.label: assign
edges.caption: Give each entity one job. The garage hands out slots; a ticket only records a visit.

edges.label: connect
edges.caption: Decide how they relate. A garage has slots and creates tickets.

edges.label: write
edges.caption: Only now write classes, with private state and a few public methods.

code.title: A tiny design
code.caption: Two classes, one job each. Add a `leave(ticket)` method that frees the slot, then run again.

quiz.q: Which question belongs to low-level design?
options: Should orders live in Postgres or MongoDB?
How many servers sit behind the load balancer?
Should `Garage` or `Ticket` decide which slot is free?
Which cloud region hosts the service?
quiz.why: Low-level design assigns responsibilities to classes inside one service. Databases, servers and regions are high-level design choices.

takeaway: Low-level design gives every class one job and a clear way to talk.
